Android Studio is the official tool Google gives developers for building Android apps. It bundles an editor, the Android SDK (the libraries and build tools every app needs), an emulator that runs a virtual phone on your computer, and Gradle, the build system that turns your code into an installable app. It is also big: expect a download of roughly 1 GB for the installer and several more gigabytes for the SDK during setup. Do this before the first class, on a good internet connection, so class time goes to writing apps instead of watching progress bars.

Check your computer first

Android Studio runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Google's published minimums are:

Windows macOS Linux
OS 64-bit Windows 10 or newer macOS 12 or newer 64-bit distro with GNOME, KDE, or Unity; glibc 2.31+
RAM 8 GB for Studio, 16 GB to also run the emulator same same
Free disk 8 GB, 16 GB with the emulator (SSD strongly preferred) same same
CPU x86_64 with virtualization (Intel VT-x or AMD-V) Apple M-series, or 6th-gen Intel Core or newer x86_64 with virtualization
Screen 1280 x 800 minimum same same

Windows and Linux computers with ARM processors are not supported yet. A Chromebook can run Android Studio only through its Linux environment, and it needs the same RAM and disk as a Linux machine.

To find your RAM:

  • Windows: open Task Manager (Ctrl + Shift + Esc), go to Performance, click Memory. While you're there, click CPU and look for Virtualization: Enabled.
  • macOS: Apple menu, About This Mac. It shows your chip (Apple M1, M2, and so on, or Intel) and memory.
  • Linux: run these two commands in a terminal.

The first prints a table; read the total value in the Mem: row. The second counts CPU cores that support hardware virtualization. Any number above 0 means the emulator can be accelerated; 0 means virtualization is missing or switched off in your BIOS.

Tip

Only 8 GB of RAM? You can still take this class. Install Android Studio, skip creating a heavy emulator, and run your apps on a real Android phone over USB instead. That uses far less memory than a virtual device.

Download

Go to the Android Studio download page (linked at the bottom) and accept the license. Pick the right file:

  • Windows: the .exe installer.
  • macOS: the .dmg for Mac with Apple chip or Mac with Intel chip. The wrong one will either refuse to open or run painfully slowly, so check About This Mac first.
  • Linux: the .tar.gz archive.

Install on Windows

  1. Double-click the .exe.
  2. On the components screen, leave Android Virtual Device checked. That is the emulator.
  3. Accept the default install folder and finish. Launch Android Studio from the Start menu.

Install on macOS

  1. Open the .dmg.
  2. Drag Android Studio into the Applications folder.
  3. Open it from Applications. macOS asks whether you trust an app downloaded from the internet; click Open.

Install on Linux

Unpack the archive somewhere permanent, then start the launcher script from the bin folder. Adjust the file name to match your download:

Recent releases also include a launcher named just studio in the same folder; either one works. Once Android Studio is open, choose Tools > Create Desktop Entry so it shows up in your app menu. On 64-bit Ubuntu, Google also asks you to install a few 32-bit libraries:

Run the setup wizard

The first launch opens a setup wizard. Choose these options:

  1. Import settings: "Do not import" (unless you've used Android Studio before).
  2. Install type: Standard. It picks sensible defaults for the SDK, the emulator, and a recent Android version.
  3. UI theme: your choice.
  4. License agreement: click each license in the left list and select Accept for every one. The Next button stays grey until all of them are accepted, which confuses a lot of people.
  5. Click Finish and let it download. On a slow connection this can take 20 minutes or more.

When it ends, you land on the Welcome to Android Studio window with buttons for New Project, Open, and More Actions. That window means the install worked.

The wizard saves the SDK here by default. Remember the path; you'll need it if something breaks later:

OS Default SDK location
Windows C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Local\Android\Sdk
macOS ~/Library/Android/sdk
Linux ~/Android/Sdk

Watch out

Avoid putting the SDK or your projects in a folder whose path has spaces or non-English characters, such as a Windows user name like Zoë Kim. Some build tools break on those paths with confusing errors. If your user name has them, create a folder like C:\Android\Sdk and point the wizard there.

One more tool for Week 2: a JDK

Android Studio ships its own Java runtime for building apps, so you never install Java just to make Android apps. In Week 2, though, you'll run small plain-Java programs from a terminal, which needs a separate JDK. Install Eclipse Temurin 21 (LTS) from adoptium.net, then open a new terminal and check it:

Both should report version 21, for example:

Your exact build numbers may differ. If you see command not found or 'java' is not recognized, close and reopen the terminal; on Windows, rerun the installer and make sure Set JAVA_HOME and Add to PATH are selected.

An installed IDE proves nothing until it builds something. Here you'll create a real project, give it a device to run on, and watch "Hello World!" appear on a phone screen. Then you'll change one line and run it again, which proves the whole chain works: your edit, the Gradle build, the install, and the launch.

Create the project

  1. On the Welcome window, click New Project. (If a project is already open, use File > New > New Project.)
  2. Under Phone and Tablet, choose Empty Views Activity and click Next. Be careful here: the template called just Empty Activity uses Jetpack Compose and Kotlin, which this class does not use.
  3. Fill in the form:
    • Name: HelloC4T
    • Package name: com.example.helloc4t (filled in for you)
    • Save location: leave the default AndroidStudioProjects folder
    • Language: Java
    • Minimum SDK: API 24 ("Nougat"; Android 7.0)
    • Build configuration language: Kotlin DSL (build.gradle.kts), the recommended default
  4. Click Finish.

The build files will be written in Kotlin DSL even though your app code is Java. That is normal for every new project now: Gradle's configuration language and your app's language are separate choices, and you'll only touch the build files occasionally.

Android Studio now runs its first Gradle sync, which downloads the libraries the template depends on. Watch the progress bar at the bottom of the window. The first sync on a new install can take several minutes. Wait for it to finish before you click anything else.

Look at what you got

Open app > java > com.example.helloc4t > MainActivity.java. The template writes this:

The key line is setContentView(R.layout.activity_main): it tells Android which screen layout to show. The inset code pads the screen so your content doesn't hide under the status bar. You'll see what each part means in Week 1.

Now open app > res > layout > activity_main.xml. If it opens as a picture of a phone, click Code (or Split) in the top-right corner of the editor:

Option A: create an emulator

An emulator is a virtual Android phone that runs in a window on your computer.

  1. Open Device Manager from the right-hand toolbar, or View > Tool Windows > Device Manager.
  2. Click + and choose Create Virtual Device.
  3. Pick a phone such as Pixel 8 and click Next.
  4. Choose a system image. Pick a recent API level with a download icon next to it, and let it download. On an Apple-silicon Mac the image must be arm64; on Intel or AMD computers it must be x86_64. Android Studio usually filters to the right kind for you.
  5. Click Finish. The device appears in the Device Manager list.
  6. Click the play button next to it. The first boot is slow, often a minute or two.

Option B: use your own Android phone

A real phone is faster than an emulator and costs your computer almost no memory.

  1. On the phone, open Settings > About phone and tap Build number seven times. You'll see "You are now a developer!" (On some brands, Build number is under Software information.)
  2. Go back to Settings, open System > Developer options, and turn on USB debugging.
  3. Plug the phone into your computer with a USB cable that carries data, not just power.
  4. The phone shows Allow USB debugging? Tick Always allow from this computer and tap Allow.

On Windows, some phones also need the manufacturer's USB driver before they show up; the OEM USB drivers page below lists them.

Run it

Pick your emulator or phone in the device dropdown on the toolbar, then click the green Run triangle (Shift + F10 on Windows and Linux, Control + R on macOS).

Gradle builds the app, installs it on the device, and starts it. On an emulator, the screen appears inside Android Studio's Running Devices panel. You should see a white screen with Hello World! in the middle.

Prove you control it

Close any doubt that you're seeing the template rather than your own work. In activity_main.xml, change the text line to use your name:

Click Run again. In a few seconds the screen updates to show the new message. Find the app on the device's home screen or app drawer, too: it has the green Android icon and the label HelloC4T.

Prove your JDK works, too

Create a file named Hello.java anywhere outside your Android project, for example on your Desktop:

In a terminal in that folder, compile and run it:

The second line shows whichever Java version you installed. If both your app and this program run, your setup is complete.

Watch out

If Run is greyed out or the dropdown says No Devices, the emulator hasn't finished booting or the phone isn't authorized. Wait for the emulator's home screen to appear, or unplug and replug the phone and look for the Allow USB debugging prompt.

Almost every Android setup problem falls into one of three buckets: Gradle can't finish syncing, the emulator can't get hardware acceleration, or the computer runs out of memory. Each has a short list of fixes, collected below. First, a quick look at how the class itself runs.

How the class works

The class meets live online once a week for 1.5 hours, for six weeks. A typical session goes like this:

  1. A short review of last week, with time for questions.
  2. The new concepts, explained with code on screen.
  3. A code-along: you build a small app alongside the instructor, step by step.
  4. Practice time, where you start the week's exercises and ask for help.

Each week on this site has three matching pages: Notes (the concepts), Code-along (the app you build), and Practice (exercises with solutions you can reveal). If you miss a class, those three pages cover what happened.

To keep class time for coding:

  • Open Android Studio before class starts and boot your emulator. A cold emulator can take two minutes, and nobody wants to wait for that live.
  • Keep your camera and mic etiquette simple: mute unless you're talking, and unmute when you're stuck. Getting stuck out loud is how everyone learns.
  • When you ask for help, share your screen with the error visible. "It doesn't work" is hard to fix; a red error message usually tells the instructor exactly what's wrong in seconds.

Saving and organizing your work

Android Studio saves files automatically as you type, so there's no Save button to forget. What matters is where your projects live and how you name them.

  • Keep every project in the default AndroidStudioProjects folder in your home directory.
  • Make a new project for each week's code-along, named so you can find it later: Week1Hello, Week3BusinessCard, and so on. Reusing one project for everything makes it hard to look back at earlier work.
  • To send a project to an instructor or move it to another computer, use File > Export > Export to Zip File.... It leaves out the large build folders, which are regenerated automatically.
  • To reopen a project, use File > Open and select the project's top folder (the one containing settings.gradle.kts), not the app folder inside it.

Tip

If you know Git, use VCS > Enable Version Control Integration (or Git in newer menus) and commit after each class. A project made by the template already includes a sensible .gitignore.

Problem 1: Gradle sync fails

Symptoms: a red banner saying Gradle sync failed, errors in the Build window, or red underlines on every import androidx... line.

Work through these in order:

  1. Check your internet connection. The first sync downloads libraries. School and work networks sometimes block those downloads; try home Wi-Fi or a phone hotspot.
  2. Sync again. Use File > Sync Project with Gradle Files. A sync interrupted halfway often succeeds on the second try.
  3. Check the Gradle JDK. Open Settings (Android Studio > Settings on macOS) and go to Build, Execution, Deployment > Build Tools > Gradle. Set Gradle JDK to the bundled one, usually labeled jbr-21 or "Embedded JDK". A wrong or missing JDK here causes errors like Unsupported class file major version.
  4. Clear caches. File > Invalidate Caches..., tick everything, then Invalidate and Restart.
  5. Read the first error, not the last. In the Build window, click the top red line. The real cause is almost always there.

Problem 2: the emulator is slow or won't start

The emulator needs your CPU's virtualization features. Without them it either refuses to start or runs so slowly it's unusable.

  • Windows: Restart into your BIOS/UEFI settings (often F2, F10, or Del while booting) and enable Intel Virtualization Technology (VT-x) or AMD SVM. Then open Turn Windows features on or off, tick Windows Hypervisor Platform, and restart. Task Manager's CPU page should now say Virtualization: Enabled.
  • macOS: Apple-silicon and recent Intel Macs have acceleration built in. If an emulator won't boot, make sure its system image is arm64 on an Apple chip.
  • Linux: the emulator uses KVM. Install it and add yourself to the kvm group, then log out and back in:

The emulator can check acceleration for you. Run it from the SDK's emulator folder (the path below is the Linux default; use your own SDK location from the install lesson):

When everything is right, the output includes a line saying KVM (on Linux), WHPX (on Windows), or Hypervisor.Framework (on macOS) is installed and usable.

Problem 3: not enough memory

If your computer freezes or the emulator closes itself during builds, you're out of RAM.

  • Close browser tabs, games, and video calls you don't need. Chrome alone can use several gigabytes.
  • Lower the emulator's memory: in Device Manager, open the device's menu, choose Edit, then the advanced settings, and set RAM to 2 GB.
  • Turn on File > Power Save Mode while you're not actively typing code; it stops background analysis.
  • Best of all, use your phone (see the previous lesson) and don't run an emulator at all.

Checking devices from the terminal

When Android Studio insists there's no device, adb (Android Debug Bridge, in the SDK's platform-tools folder) gives a straight answer. On macOS with the default SDK path:

A healthy result lists each device with the word device:

If a phone shows unauthorized instead, unlock it and accept the Allow USB debugging? prompt. If nothing is listed, try a different cable or USB port.

Watch out

Don't fix a broken setup by downloading random SDK folders or Gradle files from forums. Almost every problem above is solved inside Android Studio's own settings, and copied files usually create new errors.

A brand-new Empty Views Activity project already contains dozens of files, and almost none of them are there by accident. Knowing which ones you edit every day, which ones you edit occasionally, and which ones you never touch is what makes Android Studio feel manageable instead of overwhelming.

The Android view of your project

The Project panel on the left has a dropdown at the top. Keep it on Android. That view groups files by purpose instead of showing the raw folders on disk:

Three areas matter most: java holds your code, res holds everything that isn't code (layouts, text, colors, images), and manifests describes the app to the Android system. Gradle Scripts control how it all gets built.

MainActivity.java: the screen's code

An Activity is one screen of an app plus the Java code behind it. Here's the template's activity again, this time with comments explaining each piece:

Notice that you never write main() in an Android app. Android creates your Activity object and calls onCreate() for you. That's a big shift from console programs: your code reacts to the system instead of running top to bottom.

Every androidx... import comes from AndroidX, Google's modern support libraries. If you see an old tutorial importing android.support.v7..., it's from before 2018 and won't compile in a new project.

R: the bridge between code and resources

R.layout.activity_main and R.id.main aren't variables you wrote. Every time you build, Android generates a class named R with an integer ID for every resource. Add res/layout/settings.xml and R.layout.settings exists after the next build. Give a view android:id="@+id/main" and R.id.main appears. The + in @+id means "create this ID if it doesn't exist yet."

This is also why a typo in a resource file can break your Java: if the XML fails to compile, R isn't regenerated, and every line using it turns red.

res/layout/activity_main.xml: what the screen looks like

Layouts describe the screen in XML. Each tag is a View (something visible, like TextView) or a ViewGroup that arranges other views (like ConstraintLayout). Attributes beginning with android: are standard properties; app: attributes come from libraries such as ConstraintLayout; tools: attributes only affect the preview in Android Studio and are stripped from the real app.

The layout editor has three modes in its top-right corner: Code, Split, and Design. Use Split while learning, so you can type XML and watch the preview change.

res/values: text, colors, and themes

  • strings.xml holds text. The template defines just one string, app_name.
  • colors.xml holds named colors (only black and white to start).
  • themes/themes.xml sets the app's overall look. The template's theme is based on Theme.Material3.DayNight.NoActionBar, which means Material Design 3 styling, automatic dark mode, and no title bar at the top.

You'll use these files heavily in Week 3.

AndroidManifest.xml: the app's ID card

Before Android runs anything, it reads the manifest:

  • android:label is the name under the app icon. It points at @string/app_name, so you rename the app in strings.xml.
  • android:icon and android:roundIcon point at launcher icons in res/mipmap.
  • Every Activity must be listed in an <activity> tag. Forget one and the app crashes when you try to open it.
  • The MAIN action plus LAUNCHER category mark the Activity that opens when someone taps the icon.
  • android:exported="true" is required on any Activity with an intent filter, so the launcher is allowed to start it.

Gradle: how your app gets built

Gradle compiles your Java, packages resources, pulls in libraries, and produces an APK, the file that gets installed on the phone. New projects describe the build in Kotlin DSL files (.kts), even when the app itself is Java. You don't need to know Kotlin to read them; treat them as configuration.

The file you'll open most is build.gradle.kts (Module :app). Trimmed to the important parts, it looks like this:

  • applicationId is the app's unique ID on a device and on Google Play.
  • minSdk = 24 means the app installs on Android 7.0 and newer.
  • compileSdk and targetSdk are the newest Android version you build against. Your numbers may be higher, and newer Android Studio versions may write it as compileSdk { version = release(36) }. Both forms mean the same thing.
  • versionName is the version users see; versionCode is a number that must go up with every release.

The libs. names come from the version catalog, gradle/libs.versions.toml, which keeps every library's name and version in one place:

The [versions] section above those lines holds the actual version numbers. Dashes in catalog names become dots in Kotlin, so android-application is used as libs.plugins.android.application.

Watch out

Whenever you edit a Gradle file, a yellow bar appears saying the files have changed. Click Sync Now. Building with unsynced Gradle files is a common source of "cannot resolve symbol" errors.

What happens when you press Run

  1. Gradle generates R, compiles your Java, and merges your manifest with the libraries' manifests.
  2. Everything is packaged into a debug APK and signed with a debug key Android Studio creates for you.
  3. The APK is installed on the device you chose in the dropdown.
  4. Android reads the manifest, finds the LAUNCHER Activity, creates a MainActivity, and calls onCreate().

If a change doesn't seem to show up, it's usually because step 1 failed quietly. Open the Build window at the bottom to check.

The Apply Changes buttons next to Run can push small edits without a full reinstall. They're handy, but when anything looks odd, a plain Run is the reliable choice.

The template's white screen with "Hello World!" is identical for every Android developer on the planet. In this build you'll turn it into an app that is recognizably yours: a custom name under the icon, a two-line greeting, and a color scheme. Along the way you'll touch the manifest, three resource files, and the layout, which is exactly the tour from the notes, but with your hands on the keyboard.

Step 1: create the project

Create a new project with File > New > New Project > Empty Views Activity:

  • Name: Week1Hello
  • Language: Java
  • Minimum SDK: API 24
  • Build configuration language: Kotlin DSL (build.gradle.kts)

Wait for the Gradle sync to finish, then run it once unchanged so you know the starting point works.

Step 2: rename the app

The name under the launcher icon comes from the manifest's android:label="@string/app_name". Open app > res > values > strings.xml and change the value. While you're there, add two strings for the screen:

Use your own name. Notice the backslash in I\'m: an apostrophe inside an Android string resource must be escaped. Leave it out and Android Studio marks the line as an error.

Step 3: add your colors

Open res > values > colors.xml. Keep the two template colors and add your own. Colors are written as #AARRGGBB (alpha, red, green, blue) or the shorter #RRGGBB:

Android Studio draws a small color square in the left margin next to each line. Click it to open a color picker if you'd rather choose visually.

Resource names may only use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores, so c4t_navy works but C4T-Navy won't compile.

Step 4: update the layout

Open res > layout > activity_main.xml in Split mode. You'll make three changes:

  1. Give the root ConstraintLayout a background color.
  2. Point the existing TextView at your greeting string, give it an ID, and make it big and gold.
  3. Add a second TextView underneath it for the subtitle.

Replace the whole file with this:

What changed and why:

  • android:background="@color/c4t_navy" paints the whole screen. The @color/ prefix tells Android to look the value up in colors.xml.
  • android:text="@string/greeting" replaces the hardcoded "Hello World!". Keeping text in strings.xml is how real apps get translated: you add a second strings.xml for another language and never touch the layout.
  • sp (scale-independent pixels) is the unit for text size. It grows when the user picks a larger font in their phone's settings. dp is used for everything else, like the 12dp margin.
  • The subtitle is pinned to the left and right edges of the parent (which centers it) and its top is attached to the bottom of greetingText. The @id/greetingText reference has no + because that ID already exists.

Watch out

Keep android:id="@+id/main" on the root layout. MainActivity.java calls findViewById(R.id.main) to apply the system-bar padding. Delete that ID and the project stops compiling with error: cannot find symbol pointing at R.id.main.

Step 5: leave MainActivity.java alone (and know why)

Open MainActivity.java. You don't need to change anything: it already calls setContentView(R.layout.activity_main), so it shows whatever the layout file describes. That separation is the point of the View system. Design changes go in XML; behavior goes in Java. Starting in Week 4 you'll write Java that changes these views while the app runs, which is why both text views now have IDs.

Step 6: run it

Choose your emulator or phone and click Run. You should see:

  • A navy screen.
  • Hi, I'm Maya! (with your name) in large, bold gold text in the center.
  • This is my first Android app. in white, just below it.

Now press the device's home button and open the app drawer. Your app is listed as Hello C4T. If the old name still shows, uninstall the app from the device (long-press the icon, then Uninstall or App info > Uninstall) and run again; some launchers cache labels.

Step 7: check the preview against the device

Switch the layout editor to Design and compare it to the real screen. They should match. If the preview looks wrong but the device is right, click the refresh arrow above the preview; it sometimes lags behind your edits.

Every Android app you write in this class is Java underneath the XML. Java is stricter than Python or JavaScript: each variable has a fixed type, every statement ends in a semicolon, and the compiler refuses to build code it can't make sense of. That strictness is annoying for a week and then becomes a gift, because the compiler catches mistakes before your app ever reaches a phone.

The programs here are plain Java with a main() method, so you can run them from a terminal without Android Studio. Save each one in a file named after its class (Variables.java for public class Variables), then:

Variables and data types

A Java variable is declared with its type, and that type never changes:

The types you'll use constantly:

Type Holds Example
int whole numbers up to about 2.1 billion int lives = 3;
long bigger whole numbers (note the L) long ms = 3_000_000_000L;
double decimals double price = 4.99;
boolean true or false boolean isMuted = false;
char one character, in single quotes char grade = 'A';
String text, in double quotes String player = "Maya";

final makes a variable a constant: assign it once and the compiler blocks any later change.

The output shows the classic trap: 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5. When both sides are int, Java does integer division and throws away the remainder. Make either side a double (with 2.0 or a cast like (double) 7) to get the decimal answer. Casting the other way, (int) 9.99, chops off the decimal rather than rounding. The % operator gives the remainder.

Strings

String is a class, not a basic type, so strings come with methods you call using a dot:

  • Strings are immutable. trim() and toUpperCase() return new strings; the original stays the same.
  • substring(7, 14) includes index 7 and stops before 14. Indexes start at 0.
  • contains("Droid") is false because comparisons are case-sensitive.
  • Integer.parseInt() turns text into a number. You'll need it in Android, because everything a user types into a text box arrives as a String.
  • "4" + 2 is "42": once a String is involved, + means "join".

Watch out

Compare strings with .equals(), never ==. The == operator checks whether two variables point to the very same object in memory, not whether the text matches. It sometimes appears to work, which makes the bug harder to spot when it doesn't.

Methods, conditions, and loops

A method is a named block of code that can take parameters and return a value. Its declaration lists the return type first (String, double, or void for nothing):

  • Conditions go in parentheses and use && (and), || (or), and ! (not).
  • The counting for loop has three parts: start, keep-going test, and step. The for-each loop (for (int s : scores)) is simpler when you just need each item.
  • break leaves a loop early. while repeats as long as its condition is true.
  • In switch, a case without break or return "falls through" to the next one, which is how 6 and 7 share a result.
  • Arrays have a fixed size; scores.length (no parentheses) tells you how many items there are.

These methods are static because main calls them directly without creating an object first. Methods in your Android classes usually aren't static, for reasons the next section makes clear.

Classes and objects

A class is a blueprint; an object is one thing built from it. Each Pet object below has its own name and hunger level:

  • Fields (name, species, hunger) store each object's data. Marking them private means only the class's own methods can change them, so hunger can never go below zero by accident.
  • The constructor has the class's name and no return type. new Pet("Rex", "dog") calls it. this.name means "this object's field," as opposed to the parameter with the same name.
  • Getters like getName() let other code read private data safely.
  • toString() controls what prints when you pass an object to println.
  • The last two lines show that object variables hold references. sameDog and rex are two names for one dog, so playing with sameDog changes rex.

Inheritance: how MainActivity works

public class MainActivity extends AppCompatActivity uses inheritance: your class gets everything AppCompatActivity already does and replaces only the parts you write. Here is the same pattern in miniature:

@Override asks the compiler to confirm you're really replacing a parent method; misspell the name and it reports an error instead of silently creating a new method. super.onCreate() runs the parent's version first, which is exactly why Android's onCreate starts with super.onCreate(savedInstanceState).

Tip

New Android projects compile Java at the Java 11 language level. Stick to features like the ones on this page and avoid newer syntax such as record classes or switch expressions with -> arrows in your app code; those can fail to compile in an Android project even though your terminal's JDK accepts them.

Before a single line of Java runs, a user judges your app by its screen: whether the text lines up, whether the buttons are easy to hit, whether it still looks right on a small phone and a big tablet. Android's View system describes those screens in XML, and the decisions you make there (which container, which units, which resources) determine whether a screen bends gracefully or falls apart.

Views and ViewGroups

Every element on screen is a View. Containers that position other views are ViewGroups, and they nest to form a tree. Every view must say how big it is with two required attributes:

  • wrap_content: just big enough for its content.
  • match_parent: as big as its parent allows.
  • A fixed size such as 48dp.

Forget either android:layout_width or android:layout_height and Android Studio underlines the tag in red; run it anyway and the app crashes as soon as that screen loads.

Units: dp and sp

Screens have wildly different pixel densities, so Android avoids raw pixels.

  • dp (density-independent pixels) is about the same physical size on every phone. Use it for widths, heights, margins, and padding. A comfortable touch target is at least 48dp tall.
  • sp (scale-independent pixels) is dp that also follows the user's font-size setting. Use it only for text sizes.

LinearLayout: one direction at a time

A LinearLayout stacks its children in a single row or column, set by android:orientation. It's the simplest container and perfect for forms and lists of buttons:

The two buttons use layout_weight. Setting the width to 0dp and both weights to 1 tells the row to split its leftover space evenly, so each button gets half. Weights of 2 and 1 would give a two-thirds/one-third split.

Two attributes with nearly identical names do different jobs. android:gravity positions a view's content inside it (text inside a button). android:layout_gravity asks the parent to position the view itself. Likewise, padding is space inside a view's border and margin is space outside it.

The root LinearLayout keeps android:id="@+id/main" so the template's MainActivity still compiles.

Watch out

Don't put android:padding on the root layout in an Empty Views Activity project. The template's inset code in MainActivity calls setPadding() on that view at runtime, which replaces your padding with the system-bar sizes. Use margins on the children, or pad an inner layout instead.

ConstraintLayout: position by relationships

Nesting rows inside columns inside rows gets messy fast. ConstraintLayout, the template's default root, lets you place every view in one flat layer by connecting its edges to the parent or to other views:

Read constraint attributes as sentences: app:layout_constraintStart_toEndOf="@id/photo" means "my start edge sits against the photo's end edge." The rules that matter most:

  • Each view needs at least one horizontal and one vertical constraint. Without them, Android Studio warns "This view is not constrained," and the view jumps to the top-left corner when the app runs.
  • A width of 0dp means match constraints: stretch to fill the space between the start and end constraints. That's how the name text fills the gap beside the photo and wraps long names instead of running off screen.
  • Constrain both sides and the view centers between them. app:layout_constraintHorizontal_bias="0.3" slides it 30% of the way instead of 50%.
  • start and end (rather than left and right) flip automatically for right-to-left languages like Arabic.

In the Design view you can drag the small circles on a view's edges to create constraints, but always check the XML afterwards; it's easier to spot a missing constraint in text.

The four everyday views

TextView shows text. Useful attributes: android:text, android:textSize, android:textColor, android:textStyle (bold, italic), android:gravity, and android:maxLines with android:ellipsize="end" to cut long text with "...". Use tools:text for placeholder text that appears only in the preview.

Button is a tappable view with text. In a Material 3 project, a plain <Button> tag is automatically turned into a Material button with rounded corners and the theme's primary color. Change its color with app:backgroundTint; android:background won't work on it. Tapping does nothing until you connect Java code, which is next week's job.

ImageView displays a picture. Prefer app:srcCompat over android:src because it supports vector images on every API level. Always set android:contentDescription, which screen readers announce for blind users (use @null for purely decorative images). android:scaleType decides how an image fits: fitCenter shows all of it, centerCrop fills the box and trims edges. To add an image, copy a .png or .jpg into res/drawable (lowercase name, no spaces or dashes), or create an icon with right-click res > New > Vector Asset.

EditText is a text box. android:hint shows grey placeholder text. android:inputType controls the keyboard: textEmailAddress adds an @ key, number shows a number pad, and textPassword hides what you type. android:autofillHints (like name, emailAddress, or password) lets the phone's autofill help; for fields like notes that should never be autofilled, set android:importantForAutofill="no" instead.

Resources: one place for text, colors, and sizes

The layouts above never hardcode a value. Each @string/, @color/, or @dimen/ reference points into res/values. These are the resource files the examples need. strings.xml:

The template has no dimensions file, so create one: right-click res/values, choose New > Values Resource File, and name it dimens:

Colors work the same way in colors.xml, as you saw in Week 1. Why bother with resources?

  • Consistency: change space_medium once and every screen updates.
  • Translation: a values-es/strings.xml file with the same names gives you a Spanish app with no layout changes.
  • Variants: values-night colors for dark mode, or bigger dimens for tablets, are picked automatically.

Tip

Android Studio highlights hardcoded text in yellow. Put the cursor on it, press Alt + Enter (Option + Return on macOS), and choose Extract string resource. It creates the entry in strings.xml and rewrites the attribute for you.

Up to now your layouts have been pretty pictures. You can place a Button perfectly, but tapping it does nothing, because nothing in Java knows it exists. This week you connect the two halves of an Android app: the XML that describes the screen and the Java that decides what happens.

Step 1: Give views an id, then find them

Java can only reach a view that has an android:id. The @+id/ part means "create this id if it doesn't exist yet."

Android Studio turns every id into a constant in the generated R class, so @+id/greet_button becomes R.id.greet_button. In onCreate, after setContentView, you look views up:

findViewById searches the layout you just set. Call it before setContentView and it returns null, because there is no layout to search yet.

Watch out

A NullPointerException on a line like greetButton.setOnClickListener(...) almost always means the id is misspelled, belongs to a different layout file, or you called findViewById before setContentView.

Optional: View Binding

View Binding generates a class with one field per view, so you never type an id twice. Turn it on in app/build.gradle.kts, inside the android { } block, then click Sync Now:

For activity_main.xml you get ActivityMainBinding, and ids written in snake_case become camelCase fields:

It is type-safe and can't return null for a missing view. This course uses findViewById in examples because it shows exactly what is going on, but either style is fine in your projects.

Step 2: React to taps

A click listener is an object with one method, onClick(View v), that Android calls when the view is tapped. Java lambdas make it short:

A few things to notice:

  • getText() returns an Editable, not a String. Add .toString().
  • trim() removes stray spaces, so " " counts as empty.
  • setError shows a small red message on the field itself. It's a better way to point at the problem than a popup.
  • Toast.makeText(context, text, duration) builds a short message at the bottom of the screen, and .show() actually displays it. Forgetting .show() is the classic Toast bug.

Inside a lambda, this still means the Activity, so Toast.makeText(this, ...) works. With an old-style anonymous class (new View.OnClickListener() { ... }) you'd need MainActivity.this instead.

Step 3: Parse numbers without crashing

android:inputType="numberDecimal" shows a number keyboard, but the field can still be empty, or hold just ".". Double.parseDouble("") throws a NumberFormatException, and an uncaught exception crashes the app. Wrap the parse in try/catch:

That is plain Java, so you can test it with javac before you put it in an app. In the app, you check for -1 and call setError instead of crashing.

Step 4: The Activity lifecycle

An Activity doesn't just "run." Android moves it through states and calls a method each time:

  • onCreate: the Activity is created. Call setContentView, find views, set listeners.
  • onStart: it's becoming visible. Start things the user can see.
  • onResume: it's in front and receiving taps. Resume animations or sensors.
  • onPause: it's losing focus (a dialog or another app on top). Pause quick work.

Open your contacts, messages, or music app and you'll find the same shape: a long scrolling list, and tapping a row opens a detail screen. That pattern covers a huge share of real apps, and this week you'll learn both halves of it.

Why not just stack TextViews?

You could put 500 TextViews in a ScrollView, but Android would create all 500 views up front, even though only about 10 fit on screen. That wastes memory and makes the app slow to open.

RecyclerView creates just enough row views to fill the screen, plus a couple extra. When a row scrolls off the top, RecyclerView recycles it: it takes the same view object, fills it with the next item's data, and moves it to the bottom. Scrolling through 500 items might only ever create a dozen row views.

The four pieces

A RecyclerView always needs these four parts:

  1. Item layout: an XML file for one row.
  2. ViewHolder: a small class that holds the views inside one row, so you call findViewById once per row instead of on every scroll.
  3. Adapter: the bridge between your data (like a List<String>) and the rows. It creates ViewHolders and fills them.
  4. LayoutManager: decides how rows are arranged. LinearLayoutManager gives a vertical list.

  • onBindViewHolder puts the data for position into an existing row. It runs every time a row scrolls into view.

This week covers the last three skills a real app needs: remembering data for good, finding out why something broke, and getting the app onto someone else's phone.

SharedPreferences: a tiny saved dictionary

SharedPreferences stores key-value pairs in a private file inside your app's storage. It's perfect for settings, a high score, a username, or a short note. It is not meant for big data like hundreds of records or photos; those belong in a database or files.

Opening the file

Inside an Activity:

  • "settings" is the file name. Use the same name everywhere you read or write.
  • MODE_PRIVATE means only your app can read it. It's the only mode you should use.

Import android.content.SharedPreferences.

Writing

Changes go through an Editor. Chain the put calls and finish with apply():

apply() updates the in-memory copy right away and writes the file in the background, so it never freezes the screen. There's also commit(), which writes immediately and returns true or false, but it blocks the main thread while it works. Use apply() unless you truly need the result.

Watch out

Forgetting apply() is the number one SharedPreferences bug. prefs.edit().putString("username", "Ana"); compiles and runs, but nothing is saved.

Reading

Every getter takes a key and a default that's returned when nothing is saved yet:

The type has to match: saving with putInt and reading with getString throws a ClassCastException. Keep keys in constants (private static final String KEY_USERNAME = "username";) so a typo can't create a second, empty key.

A common pattern is to read in onCreate and write whenever the value changes, or in onPause so nothing is lost if the user leaves suddenly.

To wipe saved data while testing, go to the phone's Settings > Apps > your app > Storage > Clear storage, or just uninstall the app.

Logcat: let your app talk to you

System.out.println technically works on Android, but the proper tool is android.util.Log:

The letter is the level: v verbose, d debug, i info, w warning, e error. The tag labels where the message came from; the convention is one constant per class.

Open View > Tool Windows > Logcat while the app runs. Logcat shows messages from the whole phone, so filter it in the search bar:

  • package:mine shows only your app.
  • tag:ScoreKeeper shows only your tag.
  • level:WARN shows warnings and errors only.
  • Combine them: package:mine level:ERROR.

Reading a crash

When an app crashes, Logcat prints a stack trace in red. Here is a typical one (your numbers will differ):

How to read it:

  1. Find the last Caused by: line. That's the real problem: something was null and you called setOnClickListener on it.
  2. Below it, find the first line that mentions your package (com.example.scorekeeper). MainActivity.java:34 is the exact line. It's a blue link in Logcat; click it.
  3. Ignore the android.app... lines. They're Android's own code that called yours.

Here the Button on line 34 was null, so the findViewById id was wrong or came from a different layout.

Breakpoints: pause the app and look inside

Logs tell you what happened; a debugger lets you stop time and look around.

  1. Click in the gutter just right of a line number. A red dot appears: that's a breakpoint.
  2. Start the app with Run > Debug 'app' (the bug icon) instead of Run.
  3. When that line is about to run, the app freezes and Android Studio opens the Debug window.

Now you can:

  • Read the Variables pane to see every local variable and field right now.
  • Step Over (F8) runs the current line and stops on the next one.
  • Step Into (F7) goes inside the method being called on this line.
  • Resume Program runs until the next breakpoint.
  • Right-click a breakpoint to add a condition like i == 5 so it only stops when that's true.

Use breakpoints when the app doesn't crash but gives the wrong answer. Stepping line by line and watching a variable change is often the fastest way to see where your logic goes off track.

Building an APK

An APK is the installable file for an Android app. When you press Run, Android Studio builds one and installs it for you. To get the file itself:

Build > Build Bundle(s) / APK(s) > Build APK(s)

In some newer versions of Android Studio the same command is under Build > Generate App Bundles or APKs > Generate APKs. When it finishes, click locate in the popup. The file is at app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk.

Debug vs release

  • Debug builds are signed automatically with a debug key Android Studio made for you. Great for sharing with friends and testing. They're larger and can be debugged.
  • Release builds are optimized and must be signed with your own key. The Play Store accepts only release builds (as an app bundle, .aab).

Signing basics

Android refuses to install an unsigned APK. Signing proves that updates come from the same developer. To make a release build: Build > Generate Signed Bundle / APK, choose APK, then Create new... to make a keystore (a password-protected file holding your key). Choose the release variant, and the file appears in app/release/.

Watch out

Back up your keystore and its passwords, and never commit them to GitHub. If you lose the key, you can never publish an update to that app on the Play Store under the same listing.

Installing on a phone

Send the APK to the phone (USB, Google Drive, email), tap it, and allow Install unknown apps for the app you opened it with when Android asks. With the phone plugged in and USB debugging on, adb install app-debug.apk works too.

For six weeks you've built apps someone else designed. Now you get to decide what the app is. The capstone is your chance to make something you'd actually keep on your own phone, using every skill from the course in one project.

The brief

Build an Android app in Java, using XML layouts, that someone could pick up and use without you explaining it. It must have:

  1. Two or more screens (Activities), with navigation between them using an Intent.
  2. User input: at least one EditText or other control the user fills in, validated so bad input can't crash the app.
  3. State that survives rotation: rotate at any point and nothing the user sees should reset. At least one value must be saved with onSaveInstanceState (or a ViewModel), not only views that save themselves.
  4. A scrolling list built with RecyclerView.
  5. Saved data: close the app completely, reopen it, and the user's data is still there (SharedPreferences is enough).

Deliverables

  • A project that builds and runs. A fresh clone should open in Android Studio, sync, and run with no errors.
  • A short demo (2 to 3 minutes) in the final class: show each requirement working, live or as a screen recording.
  • A bug note: a few sentences about one real bug you hit, how you found it (Logcat, a stack trace, a breakpoint), and how you fixed it.

Picking an idea

The best capstone ideas share a shape: a list of things the user creates, plus a screen to add or view one. That shape hits every requirement almost automatically. Some ideas that fit:

  • Habit tracker: a list of habits with streaks, an "add habit" screen, and saved habits and streaks.
  • Homework planner: assignments by due date, an add/edit screen, and the saved assignment list.
  • Workout log: past workouts, a "log a workout" screen, and saved history.
  • Recipe box: recipe names, a screen with ingredients and steps, and your saved recipes.
  • Book or movie list: titles with ratings, a short-review screen, and saved titles, ratings, and reviews.
  • Club or team roster: members, a details-and-role screen, and the saved roster.
  • Flashcards: cards in a deck, a quiz mode where you tap to flip, and saved cards and best score.

You can also invent your own. Check it against the brief: if you can't say which screen is the list, what the user types, and what gets saved, the idea needs another pass.

Tip

Pick something small that you'd really use. A finished, polished habit tracker beats a half-built social network every time, and it makes a much better demo.

Ideas that cause trouble

  • Anything that needs the internet (weather, chat, logins). Networking and APIs weren't part of this course and can eat your whole schedule.
  • Games with real-time movement. Those need a custom drawing loop, not Views.
  • Huge data, like thousands of items or photos. SharedPreferences is meant for small amounts.

Plan before you build

Ten minutes on paper saves hours of rewriting XML. Answer these four questions in a notes file in your project.

1. What are the screens?

Sketch each screen as a box with its views inside. Draw an arrow for every way to move between screens, and label it with what triggers it ("tap a row", "tap Add", "Back").

2. What is one item?

Write the model class first. It forces you to decide exactly what data you're storing. For a habit tracker:

The main method is only there so you can test it with javac Habit.java and java Habit before Android is involved. Delete it when you move the class into your project.

3. What gets saved, and what survives rotation?

Make two short lists:

  • Saved forever (SharedPreferences): the items themselves, plus any settings.
  • Survives rotation (Bundle or ViewModel): things the user is in the middle of, like which filter is selected, a score in progress, or a counter on screen.

4. What can go wrong with input?

For every field, write what a careless user might type: nothing, spaces, a huge number, letters in a number field, a 500-character name. Decide now what the app does in each case. You'll test exactly these in the final week.

Schedule

  1. Planning class: idea chosen, screens sketched, model class written.
  2. Milestones 1 and 2: list screen with fake data; second screen opens through an Intent.
  3. Milestones 3 and 4: input works and is validated; data saves and reloads.
  4. Milestone 5: rotation-proof state, polish, bug note written.
  5. Final class: demo.

Your app works when you use it, because you know exactly which buttons to press and in what order. Your audience won't. This last stretch is about using your app the way a stranger would, fixing what breaks, and showing it off with confidence.

Test like you're trying to break it

Run every test on a real phone if you can, not only the emulator. Touch targets, font sizes, and performance feel different in your hand.

Rotation, on every screen

Rotate on each screen, in each state: an empty list, a full list, halfway through typing, right after an error appears. After each rotation, ask: Did anything the user could see change? Common failures:

  • A counter, score, or toggle resets. Save it in onSaveInstanceState.
  • A TextView you set in code goes back to its XML text. Save the value and set it again in onCreate.
  • An EditText loses its text. It probably has no android:id; views without ids don't save their state.

Leave and come back

  • Press Home, open another app, come back. Nothing should change.
  • Swipe the app away from recent apps and reopen it. Your saved data must be there.
  • Turn on Settings > System > Developer options > Don't keep activities (the exact path varies by phone). Now Android destroys every screen as soon as you leave it, which imitates the system killing your app to save memory. Leave and return on each screen. If anything that relies on a ViewModel alone disappears, back it up with a Bundle. Turn this setting off when you're done, or other apps will act strangely.

Odd input

Make a table of every field and feed it the worst things you can think of. Testing your validation as plain Java first is fast. For example, a "minutes" field in a workout log:

Notice 99999999999: it is digits, but it's too big for an int, so parseInt throws. That's the kind of case nobody thinks of until a friend types it in the demo. In the app, use the method like this:

Also try very long text (does it wrap or push buttons off screen?), emoji, and tapping Save twice quickly.

Empty and crowded lists

  • Zero items: a blank screen looks broken. Show a TextView like "No habits yet. Tap Add to start." and toggle it with setVisibility(View.VISIBLE) or View.GONE based on the list size.
  • Fifty items: add a lot and scroll fast. Check that rows don't show another row's data (the recycling bug from week 5) and that the Add button is still reachable.

Random taps

With the phone plugged in and USB debugging on, Android's built-in Monkey tool fires random taps and swipes at your app:

Use your own package name. If it finds a crash, the stack trace appears in Logcat; read it the way you practiced in week 6.

Polish what people notice

You don't need fancy design, but these small things make an app feel finished:

  • Real strings: move hard-coded text into strings.xml. Android Studio's warning highlights point to every one.
  • Spacing: consistent padding (16dp or 24dp) on every screen, with dimens.xml if you're repeating numbers.
  • Tap feedback: rows use ?attr/selectableItemBackground, and every action gives a response, like a Toast, a screen change, or an updated count.
  • Readable in dark mode and large fonts: switch both on in the phone's settings and check every screen. Use sp for text sizes so they scale.
  • Accessibility: give every ImageView and icon-only button an android:contentDescription, and keep touch targets at least 48dp tall.
  • A name and icon: set app_name in strings.xml, and make an icon with right-click res > New > Image Asset.

Write your bug note

Pick the bug that taught you the most. Keep it to four or five sentences:

  1. Symptom: what the user saw ("the app crashed when I saved an empty title").
  2. Evidence: how you investigated (the Caused by: line in Logcat, a breakpoint, a Log.d).
  3. Cause: the actual mistake in the code.
  4. Fix: what you changed, and how you checked it stays fixed.

Presenting (2 to 3 minutes)

Plan your demo as a short story, not a tour of every button:

  1. The problem (one sentence): who the app is for and why.
  2. The happy path: add an item, see it in the list, tap it to open the second screen.
  3. The proof: rotate the phone; close the app fully and reopen it to show saved data; type bad input to show it's handled.
  4. The bug story: your bug note, in about 30 seconds.
  5. What's next: one feature you'd add with more time.

Rehearse at least once with a timer. Have a few items already saved so you aren't typing them live, and charge your phone. If your demo device might fail, record a backup screen recording beforehand.

Grading checklist

Go through this the day before you present. You should be able to say a confident yes to every line.

Requirements

  • Two or more Activities, with navigation between them through an Intent
  • At least one input field, validated so empty or bad input shows an error instead of crashing
  • Rotating on any screen keeps everything the user sees, including at least one value saved with onSaveInstanceState or a ViewModel
  • A RecyclerView list with a custom row layout
  • Data is still there after the app is swiped away and reopened

Deliverables

  • The project syncs, builds, and runs from a fresh copy with no errors
  • A 2 to 3 minute demo that shows every requirement
  • A written bug note: symptom, evidence, cause, fix

Quality

  • No crashes during rotation, odd input, or the Monkey test
  • An empty list shows a helpful message
  • User-facing text lives in strings.xml
  • Readable in dark mode and with a large font size
  • Code uses clear names, and keys for extras and SharedPreferences are constants

Congratulations on getting here. You started with an empty template and you're finishing with an app you designed, built, debugged, and can install on anyone's phone.
